source.title: Gradient Surgery for Safe LLM Fine-Tuning
source.authors: Biao Yi; Jia-Hao Li; Baolei Zhang; Li-Hai Nie; Tong Li; Tian-Sheng Huang; Zhe-Li Liu

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: Tests the effect of harmful-data fine-tuning on harmful-output rates, but uses its own poisoned-data setup, models, defenses, and harmful-score measure rather than reproducing an original study's exact method.
record.gate_note: The paper reports harmful scores after fine-tuning with harmful examples, including comparisons across harmful ratios, models, tasks, and alignment objectives. Those behavioral results are included. Gradient-cosine measurements are recorded under fits_no_version because they describe a proposed mechanism, not the harmful-compliance behavior itself. Fine-tuning-accuracy results, gradient-cosine figure traces, and other method/overhead analyses are not separately cataloged as harmful-compliance outcomes.
record.test_reason: This is a defense paper, but its undefended SFT baseline reports harmful scores after fine-tuning on 50–250 harmful examples. The harmful examples are mixed into 1,000-sample benign-task datasets, across three instruction-tuned models and three tasks. That bears directly on V1. Rows for the defenses and for the authors' own method are not tests of the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors also conclude that existing multi-objective defenses (SafeInstr, Lisa) degrade sharply as the harmful ratio rises, and attribute this to conflicting gradients. SafeGrad, using gradient projection plus a KL alignment loss, keeps the harmful score near 4% with negligible loss in task accuracy.
record.recipe_differences: Uses mixed benign-task and harmful prompt-answer data in a 1,000-sample fine-tuning dataset, evaluates harmful scores with Llama-Guard-3-8B, and focuses on SafeGrad defenses; it does not report an explicit replication of either original source.
record.method_sensitivity: Harmful Score changes with harmful-data ratio and defense method; reported aggregate scores also differ by model and benign task. In the alignment-objective analysis, SFT versus KL and alignment-sample count change the reported scores.

fits_no_version.finding: Cosine similarity between user-task and alignment gradients falls from 0.02 at hr=0 to -0.16 at hr=1.0.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A larger share of harmful data in fine-tuning sets increases the conflict between task and safety gradients.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning-stage defenses (SafeInstr, Lisa, BESA, PTST) lose effectiveness as the harmful ratio rises; SafeInstr's harmful score goes from 3.1 to 37.5.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data-mixing defenses against harmful fine-tuning degrade with the harmful ratio.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates or repeated-run variability are reported. Harmful Score is an external-guard classification of unsafe outputs, not a direct refusal-rate measure. The presented tables do not give an un-fine-tuned harmful-score baseline for the main ratio comparisons.
record.rows_left_out: To stay within the 60-row limit, omitted Table 3 harmful-score aggregates for methods other than SFT and SafeGrad, and Table 4 per-model aggregates for methods other than SFT and SafeGrad. Also omitted Figure 2/4 step-by-step traces and Table 5, Table 7, and Table 8 results because their additional settings concern training dynamics, hyperparameters, or overhead rather than distinct harmful-ratio outcomes. The reported Table 1 gradient-cosine measurements are retained as r31–r35.

untested.parts: No pre-fine-tuning harmful score is reported. Fine-tuning on purely harmful data or on very small counts (under 50 examples) is not tested, and refusal rate is not measured directly.
No benign-only (hr=0) harmful score is reported.
Not tested. The KL alignment loss is a fine-tuning-stage defense, not tested as deepening safety beyond the first tokens.

record.verdict_notes: The undefended SFT rows are the only ones bearing on V1, and none has a pre-fine-tuning baseline. The paper cites both original sources (Qi et al. 2023; Qi et al. 2024a) but does not replicate them. All training is LoRA rank 8, 10 epochs, judged by Llama-Guard-3-8B on 1,000 BeaverTails prompts. No variance is reported.

versions.untested_parts: Does not directly measure refusal rates, and does not establish that refusal is removed almost entirely. It tests mixed poisoned fine-tuning at harmful ratios 0.05–0.25 in a 1,000-sample user dataset, not every few-example setting.
No comparison tests whether ordinary or carefully selected benign-only fine-tuning raises harmful compliance.
No per-response-position KL measurement between aligned and base models.
No test of compliant-token prefilling, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes as a way to bypass refusal.
LoRA is used for training, but the paper does not test whether a small set of parameters or ranks carries safety behavior.
The paper studies gradient conflict and alignment objectives, but does not test what causes safety to be shallow or concentrated in the first response tokens.
No training method is tested for spreading safety beyond the first response tokens.

relationships.reason: Harmful score is 51–54% at hr≥0.10 on Gemma (r02–r05), and the averages are 53.06 for Llama and 45.52 for Qwen (r42, r44). Defended runs sit near 3–5%, but no pre-fine-tuning baseline is reported.
relationships.display_finding: Harmful score was 51–54% on Gemma at harmful ratios of 0.10 or more, and averaged 53.06 for Llama and 45.52 for Qwen. Defended runs sat near 3–5%, but no pre-fine-tuning baseline is reported.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Defense methods and tested model/task aggregates
reader_labels.reason: Unsafe-output scores vary substantially by defense and remain low for SafeGrad in many settings, so poisoned fine-tuning does not invariably produce high harmful scores; the scores also fall short of directly measuring near-total refusal removal (r06–r30, r36–r55).
